The pipeline sets no oxygen or pressure range for the Mars habitat scenario, so no recorded test is counted as matching its atmosphere. A test is counted for a need only if its investigation states that need as an objective, in its PSI record or in a publication of the investigators or of NASA. The team pipeline matched these purpose sentences to the needs; a match is counted only where the publications that were read support it. The matching was done by an AI assistant and has not been reviewed by a person. Every test in the PSI experimental tables used here is a microgravity test (gravity level set per table by the team from the PSI record); these tables hold no partial-gravity test, and microgravity and 1 g results are not shown here as bounds for lunar or Martian gravity. NASA's fire protection technical brief OCHMO-TB-008 says: "Material flammability in partial gravity remains a major gap for exploration missions." (TB008.gaps). Outside PSI, Table I of a paper on the NASA Technical Reports Server (Olson and Ferkul, NTRS-20130010991) gives limiting oxygen concentrations (the oxygen level below which the flame did not keep burning in the test) for three materials; for each of them, both limits at Martian gravity are lower than those at 1 g, and for some of them they are lower than those at 0 g as well. These low-gravity limits come from 5.18 s drop-tower tests, and the paper says their extinction criteria are not the same as in 1 g; the table was read by an AI assistant and not checked by a person (OF2012.table1). The scorer preset for this scenario sets no atmosphere. NASA's Exploration Atmospheres Working Group report lists 8.0 psia (55.2 kPa) and 7.6 psia (52.4 kPa), each with 32% oxygen, among its nominal atmospheres for surface habitats and says they are not requirements (EAWG.atmospheres); the kPa values are the team's conversion, and the preset does not use these atmospheres. Computed by the team's code from NASA PSI tables (code written with an AI assistant). Counts of recorded tests in the team's bins; not a statement about how a material behaves; not NASA's conclusion; not operational safety guidance.
